title: How are the market valuations for the U.S: insurers doing? - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: U.S. insurance stocks have outperformed the S&P 500 by roughly 5-7 percentage points from May 1 to September 3, 2026, which Cowen uses as evidence that markets are not pricing in a serious probability of catastrophic AI-driven tail risk (which would be expected to hurt insurers).

themes.theme: Insurer stock performance as an AI-risk market signal

insights.claim: The iShares U.S. Insurance ETF (IAK) rose from $132.01 on May 1, 2026 to $147.87 on September 3, 2026, a 12.0% price gain excluding dividends.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Concrete benchmark for tracking whether insurer outperformance persists or reverses as an indicator of market-implied AI tail risk.
insights.quote: It rose from $132.01 on May 1 to $147.87 on September 3: +12.0%.

insights.claim: The more equal-weighted SPDR S&P Insurance ETF (KIE) rose from $56.79 to $64.80 over the same May-September 2026 window, a 14.1% gain.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Confirms the insurer outperformance is broad-based across the sector, not just concentrated in a few large-cap names within IAK.

insights.claim: Over the same May 1 to September 3, 2026 period, the S&P 500 (SPY) rose only 7.3%, meaning insurers beat the broad market by roughly 5-7 percentage points in four months.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Sector-relative outperformance of this magnitude over just four months is a notable signal for sector-rotation and relative-value positioning.
insights.quote: insurers have beaten the market by roughly 5–7 percentage points in four months

insights.claim: Cowen argues that strong insurer stock performance implies market prices do not currently reflect a realistic chance of very bad outcomes from advanced AI, since a serious probability of AI-driven catastrophe would be expected to depress insurer valuations (via elevated claims/liability risk) rather than let them outperform.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Offers a market-based (rather than narrative-based) way to gauge whether Wall Street is pricing catastrophic AI risk — insurer relative strength argues against it, a useful cross-check against AI-doom narratives when sizing tail-risk hedges.
insights.quote: Do any market prices reflect a realistic chance of very bad outcomes from advanced AI?
